title: cubic blog: Plain English Review Rules, Enforced Automatically on Every Pull Request
summary: Turn recurring review comments into focused AI review rules, with three examples and practical setup steps for cubic.
body_markdown:
When the same review comment keeps appearing on pull requests, turn it into a reusable rule. In cubic, a custom agent uses plain English instructions to look for issues that matter to your team. You can scope the agent to selected repositories and paths.


**cubic ranks #1 on every independent AI code review benchmark.**[See Martian’s independent leaderboard](https://codereview.withmartian.com/?mode=offline) . Custom agents add your team's review instructions to that foundation.


## Write a rule a reviewer can act on


A useful rule names the problem, explains when it applies, and states the exceptions. “Follow best practices” leaves too much open to interpretation. “Flag a database query inside a loop when a batch query can fetch the same records” gives the reviewer a specific pattern to investigate.


Start with a recurring issue from your own reviews. Explain the failure it causes and what evidence would justify a comment. Keep formatting and other deterministic checks in your linter.


## Three example review rules


These are illustrative instructions you can adapt to your codebase. They are not results from a benchmark or claims that every matching bug will be caught.


### Repeated database queries


> Flag database reads inside a loop when each iteration fetches related records that could be loaded together. Explain how the query count grows with the input. Do not flag a loop that only processes records already loaded into memory.


For example, loading each invoice's customer separately can turn a list request into many database round trips. The rule asks the reviewer to identify that behaviour and its cost.


### Organisation access checks


> For handlers that read or update organisation-owned records, check that the caller is authorised for that organisation. Flag a record lookup that relies only on a request-supplied ID when no equivalent access check exists in the handler or its wrapper. Identify the missing check and the affected operation.


Adapt the terminology to your application and name your existing authorisation helpers. That gives the reviewer context for recognising a check that already happens elsewhere.


### Errors reported as successful jobs


> Flag a background job that catches an error and then reports success even though required work did not complete. Allow explicitly optional work to fail when the result records that failure. Explain which required step was skipped and how the caller is misled.


This rule targets a concrete failure mode rather than asking for a log statement in every catch block.


## Set up the agent in cubic


1.


Open the[Agents library](https://www.cubic.dev/agents-library) and choose **Add agent** .


2.


Give it a short name and enter the instruction.


3.


Select the repositories where it should apply.


4.


Use path filters to focus the check on relevant code, such as your backend directory.


5.


Try it on a pull request with a known violation and another with an allowed exception. Refine the instruction when the feedback is incorrect or misses the intended issue.


Comments from custom agents identify the agent that raised the issue, so you can trace feedback back to its instruction. See the[custom agents documentation](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/custom-agents) for configuration details.


## Keep the rules useful


Review the comments your agents produce. Add missing context, narrow paths when a rule is too broad, and disable checks that repeatedly produce unhelpful feedback. AI review can miss issues or raise false positives; keep tests, static analysis, and human review in your workflow.
